review.summary: SWE-agent argues that language-model agents benefit from interfaces designed for their interaction patterns, and implements an agent-computer interface (ACI) for repository-level software engineering. On SWE-bench, the system reports 12.47% resolved with GPT-4 Turbo and presents Lite-split ablations showing that interface choices, including editing and search, affect performance. The contribution is substantial and supported by benchmark results and targeted ablations, though the evidence is scoped to the evaluated benchmark, models, and setup.

observations.claim: The paper evaluates on the full SWE-bench test set and reports a concrete result for its main system.
observations.quote: solving 12.47% (286/2,294) of the full SWE-bench test set

observations.claim: The Lite-split ablations offer evidence that interface design choices matter, rather than relying only on the overall benchmark comparison.

The authors state that the main ACI design was developed through qualitative inspection on a small, hand-picked development set; how well this process generalizes beyond the evaluated setup remains open.
observations.quote: a small set of hand-picked easier examples from the development split

observations.claim: The reported results establish performance for the specified benchmark and model configurations, but do not resolve how broadly the findings transfer to other models or software-engineering settings. I inspected the supplied pages (1–25); this assessment does not include independent reproduction or evidence beyond this paper.
observations.quote: All results, ablations, and analysis are based on two leading LMs

unresolved_questions: How well do the reported ACI improvements transfer to models and software-engineering tasks beyond those evaluated here?
Which ACI principles remain effective when the base model, repository distribution, or task budget changes?
Would the main results be stable across repeated runs on the full test set, given that most reported full-set results use pass@1?
